content:
This is probably mostly a question for @Joël Riou and @Jack McKoen. What is the current status in mathlib of facts about (strong) anodyne extensions, i.e., sequential composites of pushouts of horn inclusions?

I ask because both Math.Inc and Harmonic released new autoformalization agents earlier this week and I'm curious about testing their capabilities against proving that the map

def src : Δ[0] ⟶ coherentIso := yonedaEquiv.symm (coherentIso.x₀)

is a strong anodyne extension. Would anyone be interested in experimenting with this with me? Conversely, would anyone strongly prefer that I NOT conduct such an experiment (eg because you are working on this yourself).

Previously @Joël Riou has suggested a route to proving this stuff using the material he is developing in the AnodyneExtensions folder in Mathlib. My intention is deliberately NOT to follow that route for this test. Not because I disagree that it is likely the most efficient route towards a proof in this case. But rather because I'm mostly curious about what this test says about the capabilities of the autoformalization agents.

Addition to clarify: The reason I don't want to pursue this route is that if it was successful it would only demonstrate what we've seen in some other cases. If some human experts very carefully outline a proof, not just supplying mathematical details, but creating an optimal formal infrastructure, than an autoformalization agent can complete the last steps. What I'm curious to test is whether they can develop the necessarily formal infrastructure for themselves.

A lot of people seem to be under the impression that autoformalization can be approached as a translation problem from natural language mathematics to formal mathematics. In this case, the natural language argument is well-known, but I suspect there is a lot of invisible mathematics in formalizing the standard steps. The hope in the future is that this invisible mathematics will be handled by autoformalization agents. So I'd like to see the extent to which they can manage to tackle it in this relatively concrete case.
I do think it would help to start of with a formal statement of exactly what we are hoping to achieve in relatively standard language of a left class cofibrantly generated by a set of morphisms.

For this purpose, we could state the result defining AnodyneExtension to be the morphism property of having the llp with respect to the maps that have the rlp with respect to the horn inclusions. The results in MorphismProperty/LiftingProperty give closure under the various colimits that are involved in the standard proof.

Emily Riehl said:

This is probably mostly a question for Joël Riou and Jack McKoen. What is the current status in mathlib of facts about (strong) anodyne extensions, i.e., sequential composites of pushouts of horn inclusions?

I basically need to clean up #28462 (I have a sorry-free version in another repository) which shows that if we have a pairing (in the sense of Sean Moss) for a subcomplex A of a simplicial set X, then under certain assumptions, the inclusion of A in X is a relative cell complex (with basic cells given by horn inclusions). To prove that something is a (strong) anodyne extension consists in constructing such a pairing. At some point, I will upstream the construction of such a pairing (following Moss) for the inclusion of the pushout-product of a horn inclusion and a boundary inclusion, and also for the subdivision of a horn inclusion.

Emily Riehl said:

Would anyone be interested in experimenting with this with me?

I think I would be interested in this experiment!

On a slightly unrelated note, I recently started sketching some PRs regarding inner anodyne extensions, though some of the things I want to do with them right now require the PR that Joël mentioned. Another thing I would like to use, @Joël Riou, is the Subcomplex.unionProd API from your topcat-model-category repo. If this isn't something you plan on PRing anytime soon, I could try to make a basic PR for it
Yes, you may add Subcomplex.unionProd.
I'm also very interested in this experiment! I'm happy to help with whatever is needed.

I don't have any intention to be a blocker for anything, but I am planning in a somewhat incertain future (but, ideally beginning before this summer) to make an attempt at a formalization of the Joyal model structure following the presentation in Cisinski's book. Potentially, some of the material might intersect with that experiment (though IIRC Cisinksi uses a smaller model than the coherent iso for the interval) but please do not refrain from attempting it, there is no point blocking anything on not-yet-started projects.

One point where I am not certain about this is wether this should go through the definition as in the book, or go through the "extended" version by Nguyen (here) which AFAIU allows to also produce the co/Cartesian model structure for marked simplicial set.

Potentially, some of the material might intersect with that experiment (though IIRC Cisinksi uses a smaller model than the coherent iso for the interval) but please do not refrain from attempting it, there is no point blocking anything on not-yet-started projects.

One point where I am not certain about this is wether this should go through the definition as in the book, or go through the "extended" version by Nguyen (here) which AFAIU allows to also produce the co/Cartesian model structure for marked simplicial set.

!!! This would be fantastic. Are you also planning to formalize the proof that this model structure is cartesian closed? What we need to show that quasi-categories form an infinity-cosmos is a bit less, only concerning fibrations between fibrant objects, where there is an explicit set of generating acyclic cofibrations.

I don't view this necessarily as blocking this experiment, but please @Robin Carlier let me know if you disagree. I'm really just interested in understanding whether we can show one explicit map can be presented as a colimit in a particular way. This sort of argument is completely fundamental to pen and paper reasoning about simplicial sets, so I'm curious whether a naive attempt to translate those arguments to Lean with AI can be made to go through (without the machinery that @Joël Riou has been developing that applies in the special case of horn inclusions). If successful, we'll PR these results to the infinity-cosmos repository but not to mathlib, because the mathlib proof should be the one using the pairing stuff of Sean Moss.

Emily Riehl said in #Infinity-Cosmos > anodyne extensions:

Are you also planning to formalize the proof that this model structure is cartesian closed?

I have no very exact plans so far (as I said, there are still question marks in what exact path to even follow), but ideally the case of fibrations between fibrant objects you mention should be covered, yes. The exact point to which I get will depend massively on my time, availability, etc.

And so as I said, I am not blocking your experiment. The feasibility of my project is still somewhat uncertain, and It would also probably take a massive amount of time before anything is releasable, but I just wanted to share my wish of having that model structure formalized at some point so that Mathlib can go towards having some usable higher category theory.
I have mostly cleaned up #28462 (which I will have to split in a few PRs) and added a follow-up PR which defines anodyne extensions and strong anodyne extensions.
• #28462 feat(AlgebraicTopology/SimplicialSet): the relative cell complex attached to a rank function for a pairing
• #37321 feat(AlgebraicTopology/SimplicialSet): anodyne extensions

Note that the construction of the pushout squares in the (sequential) composition occupies more than 300 lines of code (excluding some additional painful lemmas in other imported files) https://github.com/joelriou/mathlib4/blob/2ccd8e111e6bd0fdbc4db77479668a03fb9ef1f1/Mathlib/AlgebraicTopology/SimplicialSet/AnodyneExtensions/RelativeCellComplex.lean#L236-L589
The proofs that similar squares are pushout squares are completely "invisible" in the published paper proofs.
The combinatorial description of strong anodyne extensions given by Sean Moss allows to completely focus on certain sets of nondegenerate simplices, which facilitates a lot the downstream applications of this theory.
(In other words, in this particular case, if LLMs produce messy proofs, they cannot be blamed...)
Congrats. What a monumental effort!

I'm curious what you think about the "big picture," e.g., for whether it will ever be possible to formalize all of Higher Topos Theory. Do we just need to clone like 100 copies of you? Or hope for massive improvements in AI (and sufficient fundraising to have the cash to spend on the compute). If either were possible, would they be worth the resource investments required?

I think that autoformalization is going to get much better very very quickly this year and the costs are going to come down too. Whether it gets good enough to eat Higher Topos Theory by the end of the year is not clear; my impression is that AI code is quite good at blasting through with bad definitions, and this is not really what humans tend to do (we tend to think hard about definitions until we have them right). But my money is on this approach being ultimately more efficient than trying to figure out how to clone Joel.

However there is the related question here of why one wants to formalize HTT. Forget the cost. If an AI gave you 20 million lines of inscrutable code which actually did do the job, is that progress or would it turn out that actually you wanted something else? Something _helpful_ for example?

IMHO, HTT/foundations of higher category theory is an example where a very important criterion for a formalization is the possibility to build upon it in other parts of mathematics.
You don't want to "just formalize HTT" as the end result: you want to be able to formalize it in a way that would enable possible formalization of the modern homotopy theory papers that use higher-categorical machinery at every step.
So presumably this means getting the definitions right? Maybe you don't care about AI-generated proofs?
At least, if humans formalize HTT, this would be a proof that some people have read and fully understood it! (Which, as an outsider to ∞-categories, I sometimes found it is hard to believe.)

Kevin Buzzard said:

So presumably this means getting the definitions right? Maybe you don't care about AI-generated proofs?

Yes, at the very least considerable human effort should go into setting up the definitions and design.
I have no strong opinion on AI proofs, but if the end goal is to get stuff into mathlib (which I think it should be), certainly they shouldn’t be slop as they tend to be right now.

Don't get me wrong. I'm all for human-understandable formal proofs done the right way as opposed to AI slop that is useless other than as a certificate of correctness (perhaps). But I'm a bit dispairing about the amount of effort that seems to be required. Given how difficult it is to formalize the very first foundational results, I wonder whether we'll be able to recruit enough people to formalize enough of this that it's actually usable as the basis for other formalizations.

To elaborate a bit, to engage with the quasi-categories literature, students need to familiarize themselves with the combinatorics of simplicial sets, which always takes a while. (This is the sort of thing that can be explained superficially relatively quickly but in practice takes someone doing a lot of exercises to feel totally comfortable.) But to engage with simplicial sets in Mathlib seems to require a whole other level of expertise/commitment, as the formalized versions of everything we have so far are just massively more complicated, and there's a lot that's still missing.

Part of my point above was that formalized proofs contain details that are not at all in the published mathematical books. It is not just that formalization is a penance which requires adding some new layers of "invisible" mathematics, but there was some missing mathematics in the first place.

There seems to be a lot to discuss here!

For example: are there missing definitions and tactics which would make dealing with simplicial sets easy? This is not an unreasonable question, I don't think. I remember in 2018 students complaining to me that it was ridiculously difficult to prove e.g. that if xxx and yyy were the sum of 4 squares then so was xyxyxy; there is a conceptual explanation (a sum of 4 squares is the norm of a quaternion, and now use that the norm of the product is the product of the norms) and this reduces the proof to an algebraic computation. But here's the catch: in 2018 there was no ring tactic! So you now had to 20 rw [add_comm, add_assoc, mul_comm,...] often with careful precision. Then an expert (Mario) looked at what was going on, diagnosed the problem, wrote the tactic, and suddenly the proof was just a few lines.

Next: what are the important definitions in the theory and do we know how to write them? As people will be well aware, these questions can be hard. Furthermore we have got them wrong in the past (e.g. we once changed the definition of a group!).

Next: when should one care about a proof and when should one just happily accept slop? This all depends on what one wants from a proof. Of course if the plan is to get the proof into mathlib then it has to be maintainable and a lot of AI code is not great right now -- although I would imagine that this is going to change. Extreme example: I would definitely accept a slop proof of the ABC conjecture following Mochizuki! (I am not suggesting that this is a likely outcome, merely that this is an example of a situation where one doesn't really care about the sloppiness of the proof).

Next: should the formalization community be trying to fix the issue Joel raises about missing mathematics? Or is it mathematics which should remain missing because "everyone knows it will work and doesn't care about the details"? Even in the basic definitions of schemes we ran into invisible mathematics like this, with implicit identifications of R[1/f][1/g] with R[1/g][1/f] which led to a whole bunch of diagrams which one had to check commuted, even though this seemed to be never mentioned in the literature? Here my impression is that the missing stuff is far more serious. Should it just be embedded in code which nobody ever reads or should it be carefully written up? Are there extra lessons to be learnt here? In the scheme formalization one lesson we learnt is that we should not be using docs#Localization but instead docs#IsLocalization , for example.

For algebras like R[1/f][1/g] etc, there are a priori reasons which explains that there cannot be two different R-algebra morphisms between such objects, so that all the diagrams must commute. Here, this is more "the book says it works, and we do not have plenty of time to verify the details, so that we are going to trust it works": for any single statement, there is no doubt that if we take the time to unfold the definitions, do a suitable case by case analysis, phrase some auxiliary general lemmas, we would be able to prove the statement if it is correct.
On this particular subject, https://kerodon.net/tag/00TH gives most of the details and the proof of the auxiliary lemma https://kerodon.net/tag/03X4 resembles to what I did at https://github.com/joelriou/mathlib4/blob/moss-pairing-relative-cell-complex/Mathlib/AlgebraicTopology/SimplicialSet/AnodyneExtensions/RelativeCellComplex.lean#L572-L589 but among the people who would learn about simplicial sets, how many would take the time the read the minute details of the proof of such results?!

Indeed this does look like a very long argument and it's not immediately clear that there's some tactic which makes things easier (edit: actually I guess one could imagine a tactic which makes it easier to eg construct maps between simplicial complexes). I'm a bit unclear about what the point is here. Is the claim "this argument is intuitively obvious so humans don't need to check the details, they just do the case n=2 on a piece of paper and are now completely convinced"? Or is it "humans are supposed to just believe Lurie and not check anything"? ie what does the human transfer of information here look like?

Actually, Lurie gives more details than other sources! My observation is more about the other sources that I read which would only define the sequence of subcomplexes X(i) and claim that there are pushout squares, mostly without any proof. (But who would carefully read such proofs?!)
Until I formalized this, I only had a rough understanding of the case n = 1 (not even n = 2!) coming from a picture in a book.
